fields.content: By day 90, the main implementation pattern that actually ships is harness-first agent deployment, not fully autonomous coding. Platform teams put agent work behind repo-specific acceptance harnesses: unit and integration tests, replayable CI jobs, policy checks, and PR-based review. External evidence points the same way: The New Stack article "Enterprise dev teams are about to hit a wall. And CI pipelines can't save them." (https://thenewstack.io/ai-agent-validation-bottleneck/) and Harness documentation for AI PR Agents (https://developer.harness.io/docs/code-repository/pull-requests/ai-agents) both frame the bottleneck as validation and remediation workflow, not raw code generation. Practically, teams adopt agents first where success can be proven by an existing pipeline and a diff, especially flaky-test repair, missing-test generation, and CI failure triage.
fields.counterfactual: If teams ignore the harness bottleneck and scale agent generation first, they will flood CI and code review with unverifiable patches, causing trust collapse and a rollback to manual gating.

fields.content: A near-term architecture standard emerges around isolated execution plus evidence-bearing PRs. The Aether product page (https://www.runaether.dev/) describes agents that spin up in isolated VMs, reproduce failures, verify fixes, and open PRs with proof. Harness AI PR Agents describe the same control surface inside pipelines: run agent tasks as part of workflow automation, then raise changes for human review. Within 90 days, platform teams copy this pattern even when they do not buy these products directly: ephemeral sandbox or VM, scoped repo credentials, deterministic build reproduction, then a PR artifact containing logs, test results, and rollback-safe diff.
fields.counterfactual: Without isolated execution and evidence-bearing PRs, agent fixes stay too risky for shared repos and production-adjacent maintenance, so adoption stalls at local developer experimentation.

fields.content: The most important technical enabler for directed software evolution in this window is not a better base model but better tool scoping through MCP-backed agent scaffolding. OpenAI's Codex MCP documentation (https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp) and the cookbook on consistent workflows with Codex CLI and the Agents SDK (https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/codex/codex_mcp_agents_sdk/building_consistent_workflows_codex_cli_agents_sdk) show a concrete mechanism: expose stable tools and repo context through configured MCP servers, then orchestrate repeatable workflows with auditable traces. In practice, platform teams adopt project-scoped MCP configs, curated tool allowlists, and long-running agent processes before they attempt open-ended multi-agent autonomy.
fields.counterfactual: If tool context remains ad hoc, each agent run becomes a snowflake. Teams will see inconsistent outputs, weak auditability, and security pushback from platform engineering.

fields.content: The dominant narrative that "dark factory" software engineering is imminent is overstated for the next 90 days. What actually expands is semi-autonomous maintenance under fixed guardrails, not unconstrained repo evolution. Even vendor messaging reinforces this: Harness AI PR Agents target code review, CI remediation, and test-writing tasks, while the Codex workflow materials emphasize repeatability, traceability, and scoped context rather than unrestricted self-modification. The challenge is not that models cannot write code; it is that liveness goals, cross-repo dependencies, and environment-specific acceptance criteria are still too implicit for unattended operation in most organizations.
fields.counterfactual: If leaders plan around a near-term dark factory assumption, they will underinvest in runbooks, evaluation harnesses, and ownership boundaries, producing expensive pilots that fail compliance or operational review.

fields.content: A new adoption split appears between application teams and platform teams. Application teams happily use coding agents in IDEs and terminals, but platform teams become the real chokepoint because they own CI, secrets, runners, policy, and observability. Products such as Agent CI (https://agent-ci.com/) position evaluation gates and commit-level regressions for agents as CI-native concerns, while the broader Codex ecosystem discussion (https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/16329) shows rapid tool proliferation. Within 90 days, successful organizations centralize agent harnesses as shared platform services: golden workflows, reusable eval suites, permission templates, and incident-friendly audit trails.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations treat agent adoption as an individual developer tooling choice instead of a platform capability, they will get fragmented configurations, inconsistent risk posture, and no cumulative learning across repos.

fields.content: Observation: The dark-factory narrative is more exposed to control-plane compromise than the base model narrative admits. Microsoft's April 28, 2025 post "Protecting against indirect prompt injection attacks in MCP" treats Model Context Protocol integrations as a live indirect-prompt-injection surface, which means agent tool use can be steered by untrusted artifacts unless tools are strongly isolated and user-consent boundaries are explicit. That warning is not theoretical: MCP Security Research documented CVE-2025-11445 in the Kilo Code VS Code extension, where a prompt injection could rewrite settings.json to allow git add / commit / push and turn a coding agent into a supply-chain attack path. In the next 90 days, expect more teams to pause or narrow autonomous write privileges, especially around package manifests, CI config, and repo settings. Source: https://developer.microsoft.com/blog/protecting-against-indirect-injection-attacks-mcp and https://mcpsec.dev/advisories/2025-10-02-kilo-code-ai-agent-supply-chain-attack/
fields.counterfactual: If operators ignore this, they will over-grant agent permissions, and the first successful prompt-injection or repository-poisoning incident will force a broad rollback of autonomous workflows.

fields.content: Observation: Current long-horizon coding-agent evals still argue against near-term general autonomy. SWE-Bench Pro reports that under a unified scaffold, widely used coding models remain below 25% Pass@1 on realistic enterprise-style tasks, with GPT-5 highest at 23.3%; even the public leaderboard's stronger scaffolded runs top out at 43.72% resolved for SWE-Agent + Claude-4.5-Sonnet, with a 250-turn limit and uncapped cost. This says the real bottleneck is not demo quality but sustained reliability on messy, multi-file, multi-hour work. Over the next 90 days, organizations will likely expand agent use for bounded remediation, test generation, and refactors, but they will not trust unattended end-to-end feature delivery. Source: SWE-Bench Pro leaderboard and benchmark description at https://scaleapi.github.io/SWE-bench_Pro-os/
fields.counterfactual: If this benchmark ceiling is ignored, roadmap planning will assume dark-factory capability that is not yet there, leading to missed delivery dates and expensive human cleanup of half-complete agent work.

fields.content: Observation: The dominant story that better frontier models automatically yield software autonomy is too simple; task structure and evaluation quality matter more than branding. The 2026 MSR paper "Comparing AI Coding Agents: A Task-Stratified Analysis of Pull Request Acceptance" finds large variation by task type: documentation PRs reach 82.1% acceptance while new features are 66.1%, and no single agent leads every category even though OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, and GitHub Copilot all appear competitive in some slices. That implies the next 90 days will reward teams that invest in harness design, decomposition, and repository-specific acceptance tests rather than those who merely swap model providers. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.08915v1
fields.counterfactual: If teams keep attributing failures mainly to model choice, they will underinvest in repo-specific evals and action boundaries, and performance will plateau despite model upgrades.

fields.content: Observation: Safety constraints are maturing faster than liveness proofs, so autonomy will stall in governance-heavy environments. The knowledge graph is right that safety is easier to encode than open-ended progress; in practice this means policy engines, approval gates, sandboxing, and audit trails will improve over the next 90 days, but the systems will still fail on ambiguous objectives, cross-repo coordination, and economic tradeoffs such as when to stop exploring versus ship. The likely near-term pattern is "autonomous inside a cage": agents can patch, test, and propose, but humans still arbitrate priority, cross-functional intent, and irreversible actions. This challenges the narrative that dark factories emerge simply by adding better coding models to existing CI/CD.
fields.counterfactual: If leaders mistake stronger safety rails for full operational readiness, they will push agents into decisions where no machine-readable success criterion exists, causing oscillation, approval fatigue, and trust loss.

fields.content: Cross-domain analogy: directed software evolution is moving from artisanal software production toward a just-in-time manufacturing regime where the scarce resource is not code generation but certified flow through the harness. DORA's 2025 AI-assisted software development report says AI primarily amplifies an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, and DORA's work-in-process guidance explicitly borrows from manufacturing: shorter lead times and higher quality come from limiting inventory/WIP, not from starting more work. Over the next 90 days, teams adopting coding agents will discover that unconstrained agent parallelism creates invisible software inventory (half-validated patches, speculative branches, failing test shards). The winning pattern will be kanban-like agent orchestration: strict WIP caps per repo/service, explicit promotion gates, and harness throughput dashboards. This reframes the domain from model-centric productivity to factory control theory. Sources: DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/ ; DORA Work in Process Limits https://dora.dev/capabilities/wip-limits
fields.counterfactual: If teams ignore this, they will interpret rising agent activity as progress while cycle time, merge conflict rate, and rollback frequency worsen; the dark factory stalls from queueing collapse rather than model failure.

fields.content: Economic pattern: the near-term bottleneck is shifting from model intelligence to budgeted organizational permissioning. Anthropic's Aug 20, 2025 announcement for Claude Code on Team and Enterprise introduced premium seats, spend controls, usage analytics, managed policy settings, and a Compliance API. That is a classic capital-allocation move: firms are treating coding agents less like IDE features and more like governed production equipment with quotas, telemetry, and procurement controls. In the next 90 days, large organizations experimenting with directed software evolution will centralize agent spend, set per-user or per-team tool permissions, and rank repositories by expected return on autonomous effort. Control planes for budget and policy will shape adoption faster than raw model gains. Source: Anthropic, "Claude Code and new admin controls for business plans" (Aug 20, 2025) https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-code-on-team-and-enterprise
fields.counterfactual: If this is ignored, organizations will over-focus on benchmark wins and underinvest in internal market mechanisms; autonomous coding capacity will be stranded behind finance, security, and compliance objections.

fields.content: Selection-pressure analogy from evolutionary biology: the harness is becoming the environment, and benchmark design is becoming ecological engineering. SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of 500 instances specifically created to ensure tasks are clear, test patches are correct, and problems are solvable; its leaderboard distinguishes minimal bash-only loops from richer agent scaffolds. In biological terms, this means fitness is highly dependent on the niche definition. Over the next 90 days, teams building directed software evolution systems will stop asking "which model is best?" and start curating repo-specific fitness landscapes: narrower benchmark suites, mutation budgets, and reward shaping tied to local failure modes. The practical implication is that harness quality and ecological validity will predict outcomes more than frontier-model deltas for many codebases. Sources: SWE-bench Verified overview https://www.swebench.com/verified.html ; SWE-bench paper linked from the site https://openreview.net/pdf?id=VTF8yNQM66
fields.counterfactual: If the domain ignores niche design, it will keep selecting agents that perform well on public leaderboards but regress under the local constraints, architecture, and failure modes that actually matter in production.

fields.content: Challenge to the dominant narrative: the next 90 days will not produce a true "dark factory" in mainstream software organizations; instead they will produce supply-chain-style control towers. Manufacturing analogs in supply chain operations emphasize resilient orchestration, weekly stability, daily feasibility, exception handling, and compliance visibility rather than full lights-out autonomy. The same pattern is likely here: autonomous coding agents will proliferate, but most enterprises will insert supervisory layers for spend, policy, rollback authority, and exception routing. Directed software evolution will therefore look less like fully autonomous reproduction and more like semi-autonomous cybernetic operations with humans defining guardrails and resolving tail-risk incidents. Source analogs: Deloitte, "Resilient by design: The agentic supply chain" https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/manufacturing-industrial-products/agentic-supply-chain-artificial-intelligence-manufacturing.html ; Anthropic Compliance API and managed policy settings announcement https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-code-on-team-and-enterprise
fields.counterfactual: If leaders plan for full autonomy too early, they will underbuild escalation paths, auditing, and intervention rights; one visible failure will trigger organizational retrenchment and slow the whole program.
